---
title: "Root-$n$ estimation of a parametric component in a panel NPIV model with a discrete instrument"
author:
  - name: "Samuele Centorrino"
date: today
abstract: |
  We estimate the slope vector of a partially linear panel model whose
  nonparametric argument is a continuous endogenous regressor and whose only
  instrument is discrete, with $\mathsf L\ge2$ cells. First differencing removes
  the individual effect. A conditional-mean restriction cannot then identify the
  unknown function, so we impose conditional independence between the differenced
  error and the instrument. That makes the function the solution of an ill-posed
  nonlinear operator equation, which a Bierens family turns into unconditional
  moments and Landweber--Fridman regularisation solves. A cross-fitted one-step on
  a Neyman-orthogonal moment estimates the slope vector, $\sqrt n$-consistently and
  asymptotically normally and with a consistent variance estimator, whenever the
  first-stage rate is faster than $n^{-1/4}$. A hedonic application on a county
  panel illustrates the estimator at $\mathsf L=4$, reading a regulatory
  designation as the pair of triggers that produces it.
keywords: [panel data, nonparametric instrumental variables, discrete instrument, ill-posed inverse problems]

**JEL codes:** C14, C23, C26

**Keywords:** panel data, nonparametric instrumental variables, discrete
instrument, ill-posed inverse problems

# Introduction

Fixed effects and instrumental variables are the workhorse answers to
endogeneity in panel data, and applied work uses them together. A
first-difference transformation removes whatever is fixed about the unit, and an
instrument handles what is left. Both steps are almost always taken inside a
linear specification.

We relax linearity in one regressor and keep it in the others. Over two periods
the model is
$$
Y_{ij}\;=\;\vdagger(X_{ij})\;+\;Z_{ij}'\theta_\dagger\;+\;\eta_i\;+\;U_{ij},
\qquad j\in\{1,2\},
$$
with $X_{ij}$ a scalar continuous regressor correlated with $U_{ij}$,
$Z_{ij}\in\IR^{p}$, and $\eta_i$ an individual effect that may depend on
everything observed. Differencing the two periods removes $\eta_i$ and leaves
$$
\Delta Y_i\;=\;\vdagger(X_{i2})-\vdagger(X_{i1})\;+\;\Delta Z_i'\theta_\dagger\;+\;\Delta U_i .
$$

The instrument $W_i$ takes finitely many values,
$W_i\in\{0,1,\dots,\mathsf L-1\}$ with $\mathsf L\ge2$ fixed and known to the
analyst, and that single fact is what the rest of the paper is about. Sans-serif
$\mathsf L$ is the number of instrument cells throughout, and $\mathsf L=2$ is
the binary case rather than the paper's scope.

The parameter of interest is $\theta_\dagger$. It is what a first-differenced
linear panel regression already reports, and the point here is to report it again
without having forced $X$ into a line. A researcher who suspects one regressor
enters nonlinearly, and who has a discrete instrument for it, can run the
estimator of Section 3 and read a slope vector and a standard error in the usual
way.

That estimator has two steps and only the second concerns $\theta_\dagger$. The
first solves for $\vdagger$ by a regularised iteration at a rate slower than
$n^{-1/2}$; the second is a one-step correction on a moment built to be
insensitive to that error. The propensity score
$\varrho=(\varrho_1,\dots,\varrho_{\mathsf L-1})'$, whose $l$-th coordinate is
$\varrho_l(z)=P(W=l\mid\Delta Z=z)$, is the only conditional expectation the
procedure estimates nonparametrically.

Take the exogeneity condition to be a conditional mean,
$E[\Delta U\mid W,\Delta Z]=0$. What it delivers about $\vdagger$ is the
$\mathsf L-1$ contrasts between the $W$-cells at each value of $\Delta Z$, and
identification asks those contrasts to separate every candidate from $\vdagger$.
That is a completeness condition on the instrument, and a $W$ with finitely many
values does not supply one
\citep[see][]{dominguezlobato2004,severini2006}. The obstruction is a property of
the instrument rather than of any estimator, and neither a larger sample nor a
larger $\mathsf L$ removes it.

Instruments of this kind are common in applied panel work, and the two-cell case
is the canonical one. A randomised offer, an eligibility rule crossed once, a
programme a unit is or is not exposed to: each supplies $W\in\{0,1\}$ and nothing
more. Others supply a few cells and no continuum: a randomisation into a small
number of arms, a rule with several thresholds, a designation that records which
of two triggers fired.

Discrete instruments can be accommodated either by weakening what is asked of the
data, reporting a pseudo-solution or a set rather than a function
\citep[see][]{babiiflorens2025,chenq2021}; or by strengthening the exogeneity
condition from mean independence to independence
\citep[see][among others]{centorrinofeveflorens2019,dunker2014,dunker2021}.

The latter route is the one we undertake in this paper, in the conditional form
$\Delta U\upmodels W\mid\Delta Z$.

What independence buys is a family of restrictions where the mean condition gave
$\mathsf L-1$. Every indicator of the residual is an admissible test function, so
the contrasts $\widetilde W_l=\un\{W=l\}-\varrho_l(\Delta Z)$ are asked to be
uncorrelated with all of them at once, and the system that results has enough
content to pin down a function on a continuum. Assumption A1b(iii) is that it
does, and the completeness condition that reaches its linearised form is stated
given the residual as well as the controls.

Those $\mathsf L-1$ contrasts are the whole of what the instrument supplies, and
nothing in the $W$ direction is approximated. Every conditionally centred
function of $(W,\Delta Z)$ is a $\Delta Z$-measurable linear combination of them,
so a Bierens-type device is needed only in the $\Delta Z$ direction. That is why
A1 itself is unchanged at every $\mathsf L$: it is the statement
$\Delta U\upmodels W\mid\Delta Z$ about $\sigma$-fields, and what was binary in a
previous draft of this paper was the representation and never the assumption.

What it costs is nonlinearity, and the cost is not cosmetic. The equation the
family defines is nonlinear in $\varphi$, so its linearisation
$\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}}$ is a Fréchet derivative taken at the unknown truth
and not a fixed conditional-expectation operator. The sample version is then
noisy as an operator, and not merely in its right-hand side.

Nonlinearity also reaches $\theta_\dagger$. A debiasing weight that ignored the
residual could be orthogonal only where the moment is already free of $\varphi$,
and by \cref{prp:nophifree} and \cref{cor:udep} that is a design with nothing to
debias. So the weight varies with the residual, and the moment carries a
quadratic term in $\varphi$. That term is why the first stage faces a rate
condition at all, and why the condition is $\delta_n=o(n^{-1/4})$ rather than a
product of two estimation errors.

This is why the result is not a corollary of the linear theory.

On the discrete-instrument side the closest work is the cross-section version of
the $\varphi$-problem, which we solve in a previous paper
\citep{centorrinofeveflorens2019}. It takes the instrument independent of the
structural error, writes the restriction as an operator equation, and estimates
the structural function by an iterative Landweber--Fridman scheme, with an upper
bound on the mean integrated squared error and explicit guidance on the initial
condition. There is no parametric component in that paper, no panel, and no
$\sqrt n$ statement about anything.

The machinery carries over and the question does not. Adding $Z'\theta$ changes
little about how $\vdagger$ is computed and much about what has to be proved. The
parameter $\theta_\dagger$ must be identified without recourse to a source
condition, and the moment used to estimate it must be made insensitive to a first
stage converging at a nonparametric rate.

On the panel side the closest prior work is \citet{feve2014}. They analyse
first-differenced panel models with endogenous regressors as a linear inverse
problem solved by Tikhonov regularisation, and their adjoint is an integral
against the same difference of joint densities that runs through this paper.
Their operator is linear, there is no parametric component anywhere in it, and
nothing requires the instrument to be discrete.

Their non-identification condition and their Proposition 2.2 are used here rather
than distinguished. The first, that the operator annihilates every $\varphi$ when
the two periods are exchangeable given the instrument, is the linear-case form of
\cref{prp:nophifree}; the second, of which they write that its assumption is too
strong, does not transplant at all. Their completeness hypothesis is posed on
$g\mapsto E[g\mid W]$; the conditional-independence analogue would be posed on
$\Lambda\mapsto E[\widetilde W\Lambda\mid\Delta U,\Delta Z]$, and that operator
annihilates the constants, because $\widetilde W$ is conditionally centred. The
analogue is therefore not merely stronger than theirs but unsatisfiable, and we
record it as a route that is closed rather than as one we take.

On the third side, $\sqrt n$ estimation of a finite-dimensional object whose
nuisance solves an ill-posed equation is settled for linear operators.
\citet{severini2006} give the condition, that the relevant representer lie in the
range of the adjoint. \citet{florens2006} put it to work in the partially linear
model, obtaining $\sqrt n$ normality of the slope under Tikhonov regularisation.
\citet{florenslapenta2024} reach the same model by Landweber--Fridman, keeping the
instrument out of the smoothing by fixing its bandwidth.

That literature now runs without completeness, reaches strongly identified
functionals of weakly identified functions, and delivers one-step estimators of
average marginal effects
\citep[see][among others]{bennett2023source,bennett2026jrssb,chenq2021,girardlapenta2026}.
Every operator in that list is linear.

A nonlinear framework does cover this model in principle.
\citeauthor{chen2012} (\citeyear{chen2012}, \citeyear{chen2012b}) treat conditional
moment models whose generalized residual is nonsmooth and nonlinear in the unknown
function, and deliver $\sqrt n$ normality for regular functionals under a sieve
Riesz representer condition. To the best of our understanding, instantiating it
here would call for a continuum of generalized residuals, nonparametric smoothing
in a three-to-five dimensional conditioning variable, and a Donsker property for
a regularised inverse with a data-driven stopping rule. The estimator of
Section 3 needs none of the three.

On the independence side the nearest work is \citet{poirier2017}, who computes the
semiparametric efficiency bound for a finite-dimensional parameter under
independence restrictions. His examples are a linear instrumental-variables model
and a partially linear model whose nonparametric argument is exogenous, so no
structural inverse appears in either.

He then names the step he does not take: an independence restriction whose
residual depends on an unknown function as well as on a finite-dimensional
parameter \citep[\S5]{poirier2017}.

That is the case we take up, and the differences should be recorded. He writes
the restriction unconditionally and we maintain the conditional form, and the
nuisance here additionally solves an ill-posed nonlinear operator equation. His
sentence is therefore the closest available statement of the gap and not a
description of what we do.

The combination is new to the best of our knowledge: an ill-posed *nonlinear*
operator equation for the nuisance, a discrete instrument, a differenced panel,
and a $\sqrt n$ statement about the parametric component.

We contribute to the existing literature in several directions.

First, a negative result. \Cref{prp:nophifree} shows that a moment with weight
$g$ is free of $\varphi$ exactly when the two periods' $g$-tilted marginals of the
endogenous regressor coincide. At $g\equiv1$ that is marginal stationarity of
$X$. So the partialling-out argument behind the partially linear
instrumental-variables literature is unavailable here, and its unavailability is
a property of the differenced design and not of our estimator.

Second, an orthogonal moment and the condition it needs. We add to the
differenced least-squares moment a term $\widetilde W$ times a weight evaluated
at the residual, and \cref{prp:orthog} shows that the moment's derivative in
$\varphi$ vanishes in every direction if and only if the weight's derivative
solves $\mathcal A^\ast_{\mathrm{cond}}\ell^\Pi=-\nu/\pi$. That is the range
condition of \citet{severini2006}, read at the Fréchet derivative of a nonlinear
operator instead of at a fixed one. We prove it sufficient and do not show it
necessary.

Third, a device that keeps the conditioning variables out of the nonparametric
machinery. \Cref{lem:bierens} converts the conditional restriction into an
unconditional family indexed by a scalar residual threshold and a Bierens index,
in the manner of \citet{bierens1990} and at the generality of
\citet{stinchcombewhite1998}
\citep[see also][]{bierensploberger1997,escanciano2006,fanli2000}. The conversion
is an equivalence and not an approximation, so no conditional law given
$\Delta Z$ is ever estimated, and the
Landweber--Fridman machinery carries over with a larger index set and no new
curse of dimensionality.

Finally, the theorem. \Cref{thm:rootn} states that the cross-fitted one-step
estimator is $\sqrt n$-consistent and asymptotically normal with influence
function $J^{-1}\psi_\star$, that $J=E[\Delta Z\Delta Z']$ exactly, and that the
sample sandwich is consistent for the limiting variance. The studentised
statement holds in every direction, and the positive definiteness it needs is
implied by the theorem's own hypotheses rather than added to them.

The rate the theorem asks of the first stage is stated in primitives.
\Cref{prp:phirate} delivers the first-stage rate $\delta_n$, and the frontier
\eqref{eq:frontier} asks that it be faster than $n^{-1/4}$.

Read in the primitives, the frontier is a smoothness requirement on the
propensity score: $r>d_Z(2\mu+1)/\{2(2\mu-1)\}$, with $r$ its Hölder smoothness,
$d_Z$ its number of non-degenerate arguments and $\mu$ the source index. At
$d_Z=1$ it approaches $r>2$ as $\mu\downarrow\tfrac56$ and weakens at every larger
$\mu$, so a scalar conditioning variable and five derivatives clear it throughout.

What we do not do is worth stating here rather than leaving to be found. The
estimator has two ingredients that we assume to exist and build nowhere, and it
rests on three conditions we take as primitive rather than derive. Section 3
lists both sets, Section 7 repeats them, and the supplement's remark on open
verification obligations inventories a separate matter: the four forward
obligations of the block, of which two remain open.

We assume global identification of $\vdagger$ and do not derive it, and we offer
no primitive for the linearised condition either: the instrument-completeness
route that would have reached it is unsatisfiable in this design, for the reason
given in Section 2. Nor would that condition have delivered a neighbourhood of
uniqueness had it been reachable: $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}}$ is compact by
\cref{prp:compact}, hence not bounded below, so by \cref{prp:frechet}(i) a
competitor becomes admissible at a radius shrinking to zero along the singular
system.

The theorem covers mildly ill-posed problems. Under exponentially decaying
singular values the rate attainable from any source condition is logarithmic, so
\eqref{eq:frontier} fails at every $r$.

Near the frontier the asymptotics do not bind at any sample size anyone will run,
and that is quantified rather than gestured at. At $\mu=2$, with a scalar
conditioning variable and five derivatives in the first stage, the remainder
rises in $n$ before it falls and the turn comes at $n^{\ast}\approx1{,}140$. At
the configuration the supplement's first Monte Carlo experiment runs, which sits
just inside the frontier, it comes at $n^{\ast}\approx10^{58}$.

The paper is organised as follows. Section 2 sets out the model, the operator
equation and the identification results, including the negative result on
$\varphi$-free moments and the localisation result. Section 3 defines the
estimator, the stopping rule and the cross-fitting scheme. Section 4 contains the
asymptotic theory and the frontier condition. Section 5 reports a Monte Carlo
experiment that runs the shipped estimator on estimated nuisances at three
instrument cardinalities and at sample sizes that bracket the application's; the
supplement carries it in full, together with three further experiments, one at
the configuration the theory names, one at a configuration with room to spare at
the frontier, and one that varies the instrument's cardinality on the first of
those two designs. Section 6 illustrates the estimator
on a first-differenced county panel, estimating a hedonic price function for air
quality with a regulatory designation read as four instrument cells, and the last
section concludes.
Proofs of all results are in the online supplement.

# Local identification under independence

```{=latex}
% device, the identification results, the weight and the orthogonality. NO
% COUNT IS STATED HERE OR BELOW: this read "the 15 core statements" against 17
% numbered environments plus 2 remarks on disk, and it moves whenever a
% statement is added or withdrawn. The interpretation of the assumptions, the retirement records
% and the smoothness-budget table are in the supplement, and so are the proofs.
\input{../../quality_reports/theory/panel-npiv-discrete/assumptions_main}
```
:::

We ask two things of the differenced residual in A1, and the two halves do
different work. The mean-zero half, $E[\Delta U\mid\Delta Z]=0$, delivers
restriction (B) of \cref{def:admissible}, the unconditional orthogonality
$E[\Delta Z\,\Delta U]=0$;
the conditional-independence half, $\Delta U\upmodels W\mid\Delta Z$, delivers
restriction (A). Each implication runs one way, A1 being the stronger statement in
both. Only the first identifies $\theta_\dagger$.

We build everything else from the second: the operator equation, the debiasing
weight, the Jacobian of the moment, and its orthogonality in two of the three
nuisance directions.

Restriction (B) identifies $\theta_\dagger$ on its own. Under A1 and A1b(iv),
$\theta_\dagger=\big(E[\Delta Z\Delta Z']\big)^{-1}E[\Delta Z(\Delta Y-\Delta\vdagger)]$,
the inverse existing and the expectations being finite by that same clause.
Neither the source condition A2 nor a rank condition on any other matrix enters.
That is worth stating plainly rather than leaving to be inferred: routing
identification of the parametric component through a matrix built from the
representer would make it contingent on a source condition, and it is not.

Restriction (A) carries no first-order information about $\theta_\dagger$, and that is a
theorem rather than a shortcoming of the argument. By \cref{lem:shiftinv} the set of
pairs admitted by (A) is a product set, so no functional of the conditional law of the
residual given $(W,\Delta Z)$ distinguishes $\theta_\dagger$ from any other value.

It does not follow that $\theta_\dagger$ is
unidentified, the display above having identified it, and it does not follow that
(A) is idle. A Neyman correction is mean-zero at the truth *by construction*,
which is what makes it a correction rather than a second restriction, and that is
a property of every Riesz representer in the debiased-machine-learning
construction \citep{chernozhukov2018dml,chernozhukov2022adml,chernozhukov2022riesz}
and not a defect peculiar to this model.

The comparison with \citet{poirier2017} runs the other way, and the direction is
worth stating. He shows that replacing a conditional independence restriction by a
conditional moment restriction loses identification; here identification of
$\theta_\dagger$ comes from the mean restriction, and conditional independence
supplies the debiasing channel instead.

What (A) costs is over-identification. Under an *unconditional* independence
assumption the residual at a wrong $\theta$ would fail to be independent of $W$
whenever $\Delta Z$ and $W$ are dependent, so (A) would deliver a testable
restriction on $\theta$. Under A1 as stated, $\theta_\dagger$ is exactly
identified by (B) and (A) is a pure debiasing device. Solvability of the operator
equation remains testable in the usual nonparametric-instrumental-variables sense;
what carries no over-identifying restriction is $\theta$.

What we get from the conditional-independence half and not from the mean-zero
half is one identity: $E[\widetilde W\,\Xi(\Delta U,\Delta Z)]=0$ for every
integrable $\Xi$ (Lemma L-1(v) of the supplement).

From that identity, the $\theta$-Jacobian of the debiased moment is $-J$ with
$J=E[\Delta Z\Delta Z']$ *exactly*, the debiasing summand of \eqref{eq:JSig} being
the zero matrix (part (iv) of the moment-validity lemma of the supplement). We do
not assume the local rank condition such a moment would ordinarily require,
nonsingularity of a matrix built from $\ell_\star$ and therefore statable only
under A2: it follows from A1 and A1b(iv).

Where that identity stops is where our difficulty lives, and it belongs
beside it. $\Delta h$ is $\sigma(X_1,X_2)$-measurable and not
$\sigma(\Delta U,\Delta Z)$-measurable, so the same tower step does not run in the
structural direction: A2 is precisely the assertion that the pairing there equals
$-E[\Delta Z\,\Delta h]$ for every $h\in\mathcal V$, and were it zero for every
$h$ the instrument would not move the regressor at all.

We convert that conditional restriction rather than approximate it.

\Cref{lem:bierens} carries (A) to $T(\vdagger,\theta_\dagger)=0$ in
$L^{2}(\Pi)$. The contrasts $\widetilde W$ replace
the $W$-argument by the finite index $l$ and the Bierens index $t$ removes the
$z$-argument, leaving a family indexed by $(u,t,l)$ with $u$ scalar and $l$
running over $\{1,\dots,\mathsf L-1\}$; the problem is therefore
still amenable to the existing Landweber--Fridman machinery, at an enlarged index
set and no new curse of dimensionality. B1(iv.d)'s third factor on the reference
measure is the whole of the cost: no Bierens-type device is needed in the $W$ direction,
because the space of conditionally centred functions of $(W,\Delta Z)$ is
finite-dimensional and \eqref{eq:contrast} is a basis for it.

It is also cheaper than it looks. It requires no moment condition whatsoever on
$\Delta Y$, $\Delta U$ or $\Delta Z$, and no Lebesgue density for $\Delta U$ or
$\Delta Z$. That is, $\Delta Z$ may be discrete, $\Delta U$ may have atoms, and
neither need have a finite mean. That is exactly what boundedness of $\Phi$ in
B1(i) purchases, and the smoothness
and moment conditions of C1, C2$'$ and A1b(iv) enter only when the operator is
differentiated or the parameter is identified. Compactness of $\mathcal T$ is
sufficient and is not assumed; what the proofs consume is the integrability of
B1(iv.c) and B1(v).

The weight is the exponential, and B1(ii) fixes it as a correction rather than a
convenience. Under the textbook condition, with $w$ real-analytic and
non-polynomial, the converse direction of the Bierens core lemma of the supplement
fails against the maintained componentwise $\arctan$, which is odd. For $w=\cos$
and a two-point $V$ the family sees only the even part of the image measure, and
the supplement's remark on the choice of weight exhibits the witness inside the
paper's own transform.

That failure reaches \cref{lem:bierens} itself, condition (c) then holding
whenever the *unconditional* restriction does while the $\Delta Z$-conditional one
fails through opposite-signed violations that cancel. Repair is not a matter of
strengthening $\Phi$ but of adding an intercept and indexing the family over a
subset of $\IR^{1+p}$. It is \citet[Thm.~3.1]{stinchcombewhite1998}, and it is
load-bearing rather than a *see also*. We do not adopt it.

Adopting it would change the range space and redo the envelope
bookkeeping of B1(iv)--(v) throughout. We maintain $w=\exp$, which is what
\citet[Thm.~1]{bierens1990} characterises, and the additional generality is
consumed nowhere in the programme.

Identification of $\vdagger$ separates into a linearised statement and a global
one, and we offer a primitive for neither. \Cref{prp:kerchar} characterises the
kernel of the linearisation. The
obvious primitive would be the transplant of \citet[Prop.~2.2]{feve2014} to the
conditional-independence design, an instrument-completeness condition on
$\Lambda\mapsto E[\widetilde W\Lambda\mid\Delta U,\Delta Z]$. *That transplant is
unavailable, and not because it is strong.* Under conditional exogeneity
$\widetilde W$ is centred given $\Delta Z$, so the operator annihilates every
function that is almost surely a function of $(\Delta U,\Delta Z)$, the constants
included; the completeness condition fails at $\Lambda\equiv1$ at every law the
model admits. In \citet{feve2014} the restriction is a conditional mean and the
operator is $g\mapsto E[g\mid W]$, which does not annihilate constants, and their
operator is linear in $\varphi$, so injectivity *is* identification. Our design
is the harder one twice over: the operator equation is nonlinear, so the
linearised and global statements come apart, and the completeness hypothesis
that would have delivered the linearised one cannot be posed.

The obstruction is nameable. Membership of $\mathcal V_{CI}$ is a family indexed by
test functions of the *observed* residual at the trial value, whereas running the
linearised argument globally would need the strictly larger family indexed also by
test functions of the *true* residual, about which the restriction says nothing at
a trial $\varphi$. They coincide at $\varphi=\vdagger$ and nowhere else.
\Cref{prp:compact} closes off the obvious repair: $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}}$ is
compact, hence not bounded below, so A1c does not even deliver a neighbourhood of
uniqueness.

We acknowledge that A1b(iii) is assumed rather than derived, and that no primitive
for it is offered anywhere in this paper. An earlier draft carried one for the
linearised condition and we have withdrawn it: the hypothesis it rested on is
empty in this model, for the reason above. \emph{We would rather record a route as
closed than leave a corollary standing whose hypotheses nothing satisfies.}

Global identification has been treated directly in a nonlinear
instrumental-variables problem with a duration outcome
\citep{beyhum2024}. Conditions of that kind are harder to interpret than the
linearised one and are difficult to check on data.

What a finer instrument does to that hypothesis runs the opposite way to the
reflex, and \cref{def:cellsets} and \cref{prp:localise} say what it does instead.
A conflict between two cells refutes A1, and where a violation exists the cells in
conflict with a maximal consistent set are where the failure sits. That route is
available in a design where A1b(iii) is assumed rather than derived, because
\cref{prp:localise}(ii) carries no identification hypothesis at all.

Two readings have to be blocked, and each is the one a reader arriving
from the linear literature will supply. Extra cells do not buy identification:
A1b(iii) at a coarsening of $W$, together with A1, *implies* A1b(iii) at the full
instrument, so a finer instrument makes the identification hypothesis weaker and
never stronger. Nor do they buy testability or instrument strength, for the
reasons \cref{rem:localise}(5) gives. And the mechanism is not the conditioning of the
inverse problem: the degree of ill-posedness is a property of the singular values
of $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}}$, and the cardinality of $W$ does not act on it in
any way this paper can state. What the extra cells add are moment directions,
restrictions on the same $\varphi$, and the per-cell decomposition of those
directions is the localisation.

\Cref{prp:localise}(iv) is where the design earns its keep and where the binary
case is not merely weaker but empty. One limit belongs with it and is carried by
neither statement: consistency of every cell set is
necessary for A1 and not sufficient, since the diagnostic detects
$\mathcal V_{CI}=\emptyset$ and a violation that some other $\varphi\in\mathcal V$
reconciles is invisible to it, so a cell showing no conflict is not exonerated.

\Cref{prp:nophifree} is our negative result and it is an equivalence, not an
impossibility theorem. Read its condition $\nu_g\equiv0$ at $g\equiv1$ and it is
marginal stationarity of
$X$; read at $g=\Delta Z$ it is $\nu\equiv0$, the design in which the debiasing weight
degenerates and the moment collapses to the differenced least-squares one.

The condition was reached independently in the linear case. \citet{feve2014}
observe that their operator annihilates every $\varphi$ under exchangeability of
the two periods given the instrument, which is \eqref{eq:tilted} imposed
simultaneously for every bounded $g=g(W)$. What \cref{prp:nophifree} adds is the
one-weight-at-a-time equivalence, theirs being the simultaneous condition and
correspondingly stronger, and the enlargement of $g$ from functions of $W$ to
functions of $(W,\Delta Z)$, which is the class the debiasing construction actually
searches.

*The proposition does not assert that \eqref{eq:tilted} holds or fails.* Whether it
fails is a property of the application, testable through the Picard diagnostic and
through $\hat\nu_g$ directly, and we report it rather than assert it.

A design in which it holds for the weights of interest is one in which there is
nothing to debias.

\Cref{cor:udep} closes the chain from that equivalence to the shape of the remainder. If
the debiasing weight did not vary with the residual, the moment would reduce to a
$\sigma(W,\Delta Z)$-measurable weight times the residual, and orthogonality would then
force \eqref{eq:tilted}. So in any design where \eqref{eq:tilted} fails for such
weights the selected $\ell_\star$ must have $\partial_u\ell_\star\not\equiv0$.

That is what puts a quadratic term in $\varphi$ into the moment, and it is why the
second-order remainder of \S4 is unavoidable within this moment class rather than an
artefact of the expansion.

Necessity is not sufficiency here. The condition $\partial_u\ell_\star\not\equiv0$
is necessary and not sufficient for the second-order form to be nonzero: the
conditional expectation $q=E[\widetilde W\,\partial_u\ell_\star\mid X_1,X_2]$ can
still vanish by cancellation, and excluding that is the separate hypothesis O-16
carried explicitly by \cref{prp:sharpquad}(iii)--(iv). And we make no claim about
whether the moment class is exhausted.

# Estimation

Recall that the differenced model is
$\Delta Y=\Delta\vdagger+\Delta Z'\theta_\dagger+\Delta U$, with $\vdagger$ the
unknown function and $W$ taking values in $\{0,1,\dots,\mathsf L-1\}$. We estimate
$\vdagger$ in a $\varphi$-step, which
solves an ill-posed inverse problem by regularisation and returns a rate slower
than $n^{-1/2}$; the $\theta$-step is a cross-fitted one-step on a moment built to
be insensitive to that error to first order. The multinomial first stage fits the
$\mathsf L-1$ propensities $\varrho_1,\dots,\varrho_{\mathsf L-1}$, which is why
A0 asks that $\mathsf L$ be known: the analyst has to know how many functions to
fit. A4(i)'s overlap floor $\varepsilon_\varrho$ lies in $(0,1/\mathsf L)$ and is
imposed at every cell including the base one, so it tightens mechanically as cells
are added, and \eqref{eq:omegafloor} converts it into
$\lambda_{\min}(\Omega(\Delta Z))\ge\varepsilon_\varrho/\mathsf L$.

One requirement of the assumption block is a restriction on how the analyst writes
$\Delta Z$, and it is stated here because it is invisible where it is imposed.
A4(ii) asks that the number $d_Z$ of non-degenerate coordinates of $\Delta Z$
satisfy $1\le d_Z\le p-1$, degenerate meaning almost surely equal to a constant.
Read against A1b(iv) the upper bound is sharper than it looks. It says at least one
coordinate of $\Delta Z$ is almost surely constant; that constant cannot be zero,
since a zero coordinate makes a row and a column of $E[\Delta Z\Delta Z']$ vanish
and A1b(iv) fails; and there cannot be two of them, since two non-zero constant
coordinates make two rows of that matrix proportional and A1b(iv) fails again. So
the two clauses together force $d_Z=p-1$ exactly, and force $\Delta Z$ to carry
exactly one constant coordinate, non-zero: *the differenced equation must include a
period effect.* What is not required is that the period effect be non-zero in the
population, its coefficient being an ordinary component of $\theta_\dagger$ that
may be zero; what is required is that the coordinate be present, so that
$\Delta Z$ spans an intercept in differences. A specification in which every
coordinate of $\Delta Z$ varies is excluded by A4(ii), and one in which two do not
is excluded by A1b(iv).

The lower bound does different work and is not a modelling choice. At $d_Z=0$ the
propensity exponent $\alpha=r/(2r+d_Z)$ is $\tfrac12$ exactly, A5(i)'s declared
floor puts $\hat\delta_n$ at $n^{-1/2}\sqrt{\ln n}$, and the sieve-entropy
condition $L_x\ln n=o(n\hat\delta_n^{2})$ then reads $L_x=o(1)$, which no integer
$L_x\ge1$ satisfies. \Cref{prp:phirate} has no admissible sieve dimension there and
\cref{thm:rootn} is vacuous rather than false. That is not a pathology of the
propensity, which at $d_Z=0$ is a constant and estimable at the parametric rate;
what fails is the $\varphi$-step's entropy budget, which needs room between the
noise level and the sieve dimension.

The $\varphi$-step is the iterated linearisation of \cref{def:lfstep}, run on the
spline sieve of A8 \citep[see][]{devorelorentz1993,schumaker2007} at the relaxation
\eqref{eq:normconst} \citep[see][]{dunker2014,engl2000}.

That every pass is applied to a linear equation is what makes a tangential cone
condition \citep{hanke1995} unnecessary, and the point is stronger than
convenience. The cone condition is not merely strong here: the supplement refutes
it, proving that its event has probability zero, and proving that for every
bounded candidate linearisation and for the one unbounded candidate as well.

The refutation is bounded, and the three qualifiers are load-bearing: the
condition is posed on $\mathcal V$, in the levels parameterisation, off the sieve.
A cone condition restricted to $\mathcal S_n$ is untouched by the refutation and is
also unproved, as part (3) of the supplement's remark on where the failure stops
records, and in a space of derivatives the proposition
dissolves altogether at a cost in the source index \eqref{eq:muhalf} will not pay.
Nothing in the argument above needs any of that: the $\varphi$-step is licensed by
the linearity of each pass, not by the refutation.

The derivative parameterisation is available and we decline it. Estimating the
derivative of the structural function is standard in the linear problem and
carries into the nonlinear one, where it lifts a saturation ceiling on the source
index \citep{florens2012,centorrinofeveflorens2019}. Here it pushes the wrong
way. Composing with the inverse derivative operator raises the degree of
ill-posedness from $a$ to $a+1$ *and* lowers the source index from $s/(2a)$ to
$(s-1)/\{2(a+1)\}$. At the frontier-clearing configuration $(s,a)=(3,\tfrac34)$
of the Monte Carlo that returns $\tfrac47$ in place of $2$, below the $\tfrac56$ that
\eqref{eq:muhalf} requires.

We leave recovering marginal effects from $\hat\varphi$ to future research.

We stop the iteration on a discrepancy principle at a level that is
stage-dependent and deterministic, and both features are load-bearing.

Stage-dependent, because the data error of the stage-$k$ equation is not
$\hat\delta_n$ but $\hat\delta_n\ln n$ plus the linearisation remainder
$h_u^{-2}\varepsilon_{k-1}^{2}$. A fixed level sits below the true data error in
exactly the regime the recursion must pass through, and there the classical
discrepancy guarantee does not apply.

Deterministic, for two reasons of different status. The first is this paper's own
and is sharp: the realised residual cannot supply the level, because bounding the
unobservable error from below through the residual would require a lower bound on
$\|\hat{\mathcal A}v\|$ in terms of $\|v\|$. That
$\|\hat{\mathcal A}v_\dagger\|\ll\|v_\dagger\|$ is available is not an accident of
this construction but the definition of ill-posedness. The second is classical and
is cited: no rule depending on the data alone can make a regularisation method
convergent for a genuinely ill-posed problem \citep{bakushinskii1984}.

*That statement is weaker than it looks here.* It is worst-case and deterministic,
and in the statistical setting we inhabit it does not exclude data-driven
selection. Lepskii-type balancing over the regularisation index is purely
data-driven and attains the optimal rate up to a logarithmic factor
\citep[see][]{dunker2021,lepskii1990}. We therefore prefer the schedule of
\eqref{eq:lfsched}, and are not forced into it.

It is preferred at a stated price. That schedule is *computable* from four inputs and it
is not *known*: what $\mathsf c_{14}$ and $\mathsf c_{15}$ must dominate are analytic
constants built from the kernel, from the design, and from the spectral pre-image radius
$\mathsf R_\ast$ of (P-a.3).

The error is not symmetric in direction. Chosen too large, the rule stops
earlier, the rate is unchanged in order and the constant degrades. Chosen too
small, the implemented level again sits below the true data error at some stage and
the discrepancy guarantee is void, leaving whatever the cap \eqref{eq:cap} returns.
This is the one place the procedure carries a tuning constant the theory does not
pin, and we say so here rather than leave it to be discovered.

\Cref{prp:phirate} is the rate. It discharges A5(i) rather than assuming it, and it
reaches neither A5(ii) nor A5(iii), which \cref{thm:rootn} carries as hypotheses at
(T-4). Two further things we do not claim
should be read with it. It is an upper bound and not a
sharpness statement, and nothing there says $\delta_n$ cannot be improved. And the
source index $\mu$ is *primitive*, at (P-a.3), together with $\mathsf R_\ast$.

What pins $\mu$ is not the identity $\mu=s/(2a)$, and the reason is worth giving to a
referee who asks. The passage from a Hilbert-scale source
condition plus a link condition to the *spectral* condition the classical
discrepancy theorem consumes is operator interpolation at exponent $2\mu$. That is
available only at $2\mu\le1$, while \eqref{eq:muhalf} forces $2\mu>\tfrac53$.

The $\theta$-step runs on the debiased moment $\psi$ of \eqref{eq:psidef}: the differenced
least-squares moment plus $\widetilde W$ times a weight evaluated at the residual.
We compute every nuisance out of fold (\cref{def:crossfit}) and take the one-step
\eqref{eq:onestep} from the plug-in preliminary \eqref{eq:prelimtheta}
\citep[see][]{chernozhukov2018dml,neweyrobins2018}.

The preliminary inherits the first-stage rate,
$\|\hat\theta^{(0)}-\theta_\dagger\|=O_P(n^{-1/2})+O_P(\delta_n)$, and it inherits it
because $\theta_\dagger$ is identified by restriction (B) alone (the plug-in
preliminary lemma of the supplement); no condition on the weight, on the propensity or on A2 enters it. Its variance estimator
is the sample sandwich \eqref{eq:Sighat}, which carries a transpose because $\hat J$ is
not symmetric even though $J$ is.

We run the $\varphi$-step at a fixed anchor $\theta_\circ$, licensed by
\cref{cor:opsol} and \cref{lem:shiftinv} under A1b(iii) rather than assumed. What
is $\theta$-dependent is the conditioning, and the mechanism is worth naming: in
\eqref{eq:Adef} a conditional density is evaluated at a $\theta$-dependent point,
which moves the singular values of the operator and with them every constant
\cref{prp:phirate} is read at. The population solution set is $\theta$-free; the
operator is not.

Debiasing enters through the choice of weight, and \cref{prp:orthog} prices all three
nuisance directions. The adjoint equation its first clause turns on is A2. In the weight
direction the derivative vanishes at every perturbation and not merely to first order,
because $\psi$ is bi-affine there.

In the propensity direction the equivalence is with N1, conditional centring given
$\Delta Z$. N1 can always be arranged by a
straightforward re-anchoring, at no cost to $\partial_uL$ and none to $E[\psi]$, but it does not
hold automatically, and \cref{prp:orthog}(iii) is the statement of exactly what its
failure costs. That equivalence is what demotes $\varrho$ from a $\sqrt n$ nuisance
to a product-rate one. Forming the weight never requires a weighting measure on
$\mathcal T$ to be chosen:
by Lemma L-2 of the supplement the estimator solves for $L$ inside a dense class,
so we compute no $t$-integral in forming it, which is also the argument against a
continuum-GMM formulation \citep{carrascoflorens2000}.

*We assume two ingredients of this estimator to exist with stated properties and
construct neither in this paper; three further conditions we take as primitive
rather than derive. Each is named in a hypothesis rather than buried in a
regularity condition.*

The two unbuilt ingredients are estimators. A5(iv) prices the representer estimator
$\hat\ell$, and no construction attaining that rate is
supplied. The preliminary $\hat\varphi^{(0)}$ has no supplier either, the schedule
\eqref{eq:lfsched} needing it at a declared deterministic envelope
$\hat\varepsilon_0$ of polynomial order, for which consistency will not do.

The three primitives are conditions, not objects. Both $\mu$ and $\mathsf R_\ast$
are primitive, as above. Global identification of $\vdagger$ is assumed at
A1b(iii) and not derived. And on the sieve branch of the first-order bias, the
sieve display of Lemma L-7 in the supplement is assumed.

Obligations of a second kind are construction claims rather than assumptions and
are carried explicitly by the hypotheses that consume them. The first is that
$\hat L^{(-k)}$ *is* an anchored antiderivative
$L^{\,\hat b^{(-k)}}_{\hat\ell^{(-k)}}$ of a bounded, $u$-continuous
$\hat\ell^{(-k)}$, which is (R-a) of \cref{thm:rootn}. The second is that the
direction $\hat L^{(-k)}-L_\star$ is conditionally centred, which is (R-c), a
disjunction whose first branch assumes N1$'$ and whose second *prices the failure*
at $r_n\epsilon^{L}_n$ through the fourth term of the supplement's bias
decomposition. Pricing a failure is the honest third option, and it is neither a
discharge nor an evasion. The supplement's remark on open verification obligations
is the single inventory.

# Asymptotic properties

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
```{=latex}
% The four asymptotic statements.  The other 62 environments of results.tex are
% in results_supp.tex, which supplement.qmd inputs ahead of proofs.tex; the
% prose here and in Sections 2 and 3 refers to them BY NAME.  results_s2 +
% results_s3 + results_s4 + results_supp are the undivided results.tex.
\input{../../quality_reports/theory/panel-npiv-discrete/results_s4_asymptotics}
```
:::

\Cref{thm:rootn} is our main result, and what carries it is an *exact*
decomposition rather than an expansion. The
bias decomposition of the supplement writes the conditional bias of the debiased
moment at the estimated nuisances as the balancing pairing
$-\langle\nu_{g_k}/\pi,h_k\rangle$ plus
exactly three remainders, one quadratic in the structural error and two products of
two estimation errors. There is no Taylor remainder in the weight or the propensity
directions, because the moment is bi-affine there. What makes each of the three
$o_P(n^{-1/2})$ is the frontier \eqref{eq:frontier}.

The empirical-process term costs nothing at scale $n^{-1/2}$, and that is a positioning
commitment rather than a technical convenience. Lemma L-8 of the supplement obtains
$\sqrt n\sum_{k=1}^{\mathsf F}\tfrac{n_k}{n}(\mathbb E_{n,k}-E)[\hat\psi^{(-k)}-\psi_\star]=o_P(1)$ from conditional
Chebyshev at a frozen nuisance, so the only input is $L^{2}(P)$-consistency of the
estimated moment: no entropy condition, no Donsker property, no stochastic
equicontinuity at the estimated point. We make that concession once, in the
$\varphi$-step, where we take a uniform law with a rate over a slowly growing
ball at scale $\hat\delta_n\gg n^{-1/2}$. A penalised
sieve minimum-distance treatment of $\theta$ would need the harder statement at the
harder scale.

The sandwich is simpler than its construction suggests. At the $J=E[\Delta Z\Delta Z']$
of \S2, the variance splits exactly, by the same tower step applied to the
cross term:
$\Sigma=E[\Delta Z\Delta Z'\Delta U^{2}]+E[L_\star\widetilde W\widetilde W'L_\star']$.
So the
sandwich is the variance the infeasible plug-in \eqref{eq:prelimtheta} would have at
a *known* $\vdagger$, plus a positive semidefinite term that does not vanish under
overlap.

That the second term does not vanish is reached differently at
$\mathsf L\ge3$, and the binary route is unavailable there rather than merely
weaker. At $\mathsf L=2$, $\widetilde W^{2}\ge\varepsilon_\varrho^{2}$ surely under
A4(i), which bounds the term below by $\varepsilon_\varrho^{2}E[L_\star L_\star']$.
At $\mathsf L\ge3$ that argument fails outright: $\widetilde W\widetilde W'$ has
rank one, so no sure inequality $\widetilde W\widetilde W'\succeq cI$ holds at any
$c>0$, and $L_\star\widetilde W\widetilde W'L_\star'$ is singular at every sample
point once $p>1$. The route that works at every $\mathsf L$ is the conditional
one, and it is what \eqref{eq:omegafloor} was written for: under A1,
$E[\widetilde W\widetilde W'\mid\Delta U,\Delta Z]=\Omega(\Delta Z)$, and A4(i)
gives $\Omega(\Delta Z)\succeq(\varepsilon_\varrho/\mathsf L)I$.

*What the debiasing weight buys is not variance but the removal of the first-order
bias* that the plug-in carries at exact order $\|h_k\|$. That is the standard
debiasing trade \citep[see][]{chernozhukov2022lr,ichimuranewey2022}, and it is not
a defect.

We do not compare the estimator to a semiparametric efficiency bound. The bound
\citet{poirier2017} computes under independence restrictions is for a model
without a structural inverse \citep[see also][]{aichen2012,bkrw1993}, and
computing one here, where the nuisance solves an ill-posed nonlinear operator
equation, is a step we leave to future research.

No correction for the estimation of $\varrho$ appears in the influence function, and its
absence is a consequence rather than an omission. By \cref{prp:orthog}(iii) the
$\varrho$-derivative of the moment vanishes exactly under N1, so there is nothing for a
correction to remove; Lemma L-11 of the supplement states this as a property of the
limit and not as an approximation to it.

The positivity the studentised statement needs is *implied by the theorem's hypotheses
rather than assumed*. Notice that its conclusion is quantified over every
$\vartheta$ with $\|\vartheta\|=1$, not over the directions on which the sandwich
happens to be positive. By part (v) of the moment-validity lemma of the supplement, $\Sigma\succ0$
follows from A1b(iv) and
C2$'$(i), both of which the theorem already carries, since
$E[\Delta Z\Delta Z']$ nonsingular gives $P(\vartheta'\Delta Z\ne0)>0$ and a
conditional density for $\Delta U$ gives $P(\Delta U=0)=0$.

A proviso that a theorem's hypotheses entail belongs in its conclusion and not on
the user's checklist.

The scope is mild ill-posedness, and severe ill-posedness is a place the theorem does not
reach rather than a gap in the proof. What \eqref{eq:frontier} requires is that $\delta_n$
be a *polynomial* rate faster than $n^{-1/4}$, which under H1's $\sigma_j\asymp j^{-a}$ is
what a source condition delivers. Under exponentially decaying singular values the
rate attainable from *any* source condition is logarithmic in $n$, so A5(ii) fails
at every $r$ and the theorem is unavailable.

H1's scale supplies a shorter reading of that scope, and it needs qualifying. The
reading pairs mild ill-posedness with $s>a+\tfrac12$, hence
$\mu>\tfrac12+1/(4a)$, and at $a\le\tfrac34$ that inequality is taken to deliver
the source-index restriction the theorem carries.

The inequalities in that reading are statements about $\mu_{\text{H1}}=s/(2a)$, the
index of A2 at the *population* operator on all of $\mathcal V$ at $\theta_\dagger$, whereas
\eqref{eq:muhalf} and \eqref{eq:frontier} carry (P-a.3)'s primitive $\mu$ at the
finite-rank compression of the realised operator at $\theta_\circ$. The bridge
between them is the operator interpolation that the supplement's remark on (P-a.3)
shows unavailable at every $2\mu>1$, and the commutativity proviso that would
restore it is stated and declined.

Read as an interpretation it is right; read as a scope statement it both excludes
designs the theorem covers and claims designs it does not.

The rate condition cannot be relaxed by bounding the remainder more carefully, *and that
is a weaker claim than necessity*. \Cref{prp:sharpquad} makes the direct bound
order-sharp under O-16(a), so no argument that merely improves it will weaken
\eqref{eq:frontier}.

The sharpness statement invites readings that the supplement's scope remark blocks.
It does not
say that the realised remainder at $h_k=\hat\varphi^{(-k)}-\vdagger$ fails to be
$o_P(\|h_k\|^{2})$: a regularisation path confined to directions on which the form
is small could do better, and nothing here excludes that. It does not say that
$\delta_n=o(n^{-1/4})$ is *necessary* for $\sqrt n$-estimability of $\theta_\dagger$
by some estimator. And it does not say the moment class is exhausted.

What relaxing the frontier would require is a different selection, one with a
smaller $\sigma_q$ and compact part, which is open. The alternative is a restriction
on the *direction* of the first-stage error, which is an extra hypothesis and not a
sharper argument. The sharpness statement carries a hypothesis of its own, O-16, which asserts that
the form does not degenerate and which does not follow from \cref{cor:udep}. Here
$q$ can vanish by cancellation inside the conditional expectation, and
$q\not\equiv0$ alone is not enough either, an antisymmetric $q\,f_{X_1,X_2}$ making
the form vanish against the symmetric $(\Delta h)^{2}$.

*We acknowledge that near the frontier the theorem's asymptotics do not bind at any
sample size anyone will run, and we would rather say so than let a referee find it.*

Write $\hat\delta_n=n^{-\alpha}$ and $\kappa=2\mu/(2\mu+1)$. The $\theta$-remainder is
$O_P(n^{-1/2}+\sqrt n\,\delta_n^{2})$ and its second term is
$\sqrt n\,\delta_n^{2}=n^{-\beta}(\ln n)^{2\kappa}$ with $\beta=2\kappa\alpha-\tfrac12$,
which is strictly positive by \eqref{eq:frontier}. In $t=\ln n$ that is
$e^{-\beta t}t^{2\kappa}$, which is *increasing* for $t<2\kappa/\beta$, so the remainder
*rises* in $n$ up to $n^{\ast}=\exp\{2\kappa/\beta\}$ and only then falls. The
Monte Carlo experiment at the configuration this theory names, which the
supplement carries, runs at $\mu=2$, hence $\kappa=\tfrac45$, and at
$\alpha=0.32$, so that $\kappa\alpha=0.256>\tfrac14$ and the design sits *inside* the
frontier. There one gets $\beta=0.012$ and $n^{\ast}=e^{400/3}\approx10^{58}$.

That threshold is a fact about where the design sits and not about the theorem, and the
same formula prices designs that sit elsewhere. It is not an artefact of a badly chosen
parameterisation: $\beta\downarrow0$ as $\kappa\alpha\downarrow\tfrac14$, so
$n^{\ast}\uparrow\infty$ at the frontier and the $10^{58}$ is a property of
\eqref{eq:frontier} itself. But $n^{\ast}$ falls away from the frontier as steeply as it
climbs towards it, and it does so well inside the admissible range rather than at its edge.

Take $d_Z=1$. A first stage with $r=5$ derivatives gives $\alpha=\tfrac5{11}$, hence
$\beta=\tfrac5{22}$ and $n^{\ast}=e^{176/25}\approx1{,}140$ at $\mu=2$, and
$n^{\ast}=e^{352/61}\approx320$ at $\mu=4$; at $r=12$ and $\mu=10$,
$n^{\ast}=e^{400/87}\approx99$. These are ordinary smooth designs with a scalar
conditioning variable, satisfying every hypothesis the theorem carries, and at them the turn
happens at sample sizes anyone will run.
*So the concession is that the asymptotics do not bind near the frontier, and that
the configuration that experiment runs is near it.* It is not that they bind nowhere.

Nothing in this weakens \eqref{eq:rootn}. The $o_P(1)$ there is a statement
about the limit and it is proved. What changes is how finite-sample evidence should be
read. Below $n^{\ast}$ the object that describes the estimator is
\cref{cor:ratefloor}, in which $\delta_n^{2}$, $\delta_n\epsilon_n$, $r_n\delta_n$ and
$r_n\epsilon^{L}_n$ appear as *terms* of the rate and not as remainders sent to zero.

That corollary is honest about its own exponents in the same way. On the branch that
prices $\hat\ell$ directly, two of them, $\epsilon_n$ and $\epsilon^{L}_n$, are
assumed and not derived, because neither has a supplier in the maintained block.
Only on the sieve branch for the first-order bias, together with N1$'$ at each
estimated direction, do both unsupplied symbols disappear, and the primitives the
surviving exponents are functions of are $(\mu,r,d_Z,s)$.

So the correct reading of \eqref{eq:frontier} is that it is a *qualitative*
frontier: crossing it makes the remainder vanish eventually and says nothing about
where.

Finally, the theorem is *pointwise in $P$*, and this is the quantifier the finite-sample
caveats all sit inside. Every hypothesis is imposed at a single data-generating law, and
$\mu$, $\mathsf R_\ast$, $a$, $s$, $\varepsilon_\varrho$, $r$, $\bar c_\pi$, the
representer's budgets and the singular system of $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{cond}}$ are all
$P$-specific constants.

The consequences are real limitations rather than formalities. The $o_P(1)$ in
\eqref{eq:rootn} is not uniform over any neighbourhood of $P$, so the theorem does not
deliver confidence sets whose coverage is honest over a class, and no such class is
defined here. The $10^{58}$ of the previous paragraph is that gap displayed numerically:
within any class containing laws arbitrarily close to the frontier the convergence cannot
be uniform. And $\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)>0$ holds at each $P$ and may be arbitrarily
small along a sequence of laws, so the positivity established above is pointwise too.

A uniform statement would need a class on which those constants are bounded, a
uniform version of \eqref{eq:phirate} at a random compressed operator, and a
Lindeberg condition uniform in $P$. We attempt none of the three.

# Monte Carlo

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

We run the shipped estimator on a multinomial design, on the code Section 6
estimates with and with every nuisance fitted from the sample. The instrument is
drawn at four cells and read at $\mathsf L\in\{2,3,4\}$ off one draw, so the
cardinality varies inside a replication and the three readings are paired. Three
laws are drawn from that design: a balanced one; a skewed one, which moves the
distribution of the differenced controls and leaves the propensity correctly
specified; and a third that misspecifies $\hat\varrho$, the nuisance A4(iii)
prices. The estimator cross-fits at $\mathsf F=5$ folds, so the operator is built
on $\lceil0.4n\rceil$ design points. Everything below is produced by
`scripts/simulations/sim_merged_cardinality.R`.

The grid is $n\in\{400,800,1{,}600\}$ and it is chosen to bracket the panel of
Section 6, which has $n=983$ counties and so sits between its second and third
points. *That is the experiment and not a limitation of it.* Three further
experiments run the same estimator against population objects computed in closed
form, with the nuisances injected at controlled rates rather than fitted, and
they reach $n=181{,}019$ at $5{,}000$ replications in every cell; the supplement
carries all three, in its first four sections. The first of them, at the
configuration the theory names, finds the estimator matching its limit law at
large $n$ only: the simulated standard deviation clears a two-standard-error bar
against its asymptotic value at $n=181{,}019$ at one of two equally admissible
constants and at neither below $n=64{,}000$. The second, run at a configuration
with more than twenty times the frontier margin and a propensity no smoother,
meets a pre-committed coverage criterion from $n=354$ upward, which locates that
verdict in the design rather than in \cref{thm:rootn}. What none of the three can
answer is how the shipped code behaves at a sample size a reader has, because
none of them runs the shipped code. *Nor do the three suites merge into a single
cardinality contrast*: they differ in the design, in the estimator and in the
nuisance regime, and their sample-size grids do not intersect at any point, so a
table whose columns read $\mathsf L=2$ and $\mathsf L=4$ but whose rows came from
two of them would attribute three differences to the cardinality. The supplement
sets the three beside each other under a rule that keeps one design, one
estimator and one nuisance regime to a row (Table S29 of the supplement).

One precision statement governs everything below. The suite was run at $120$
replications and returns between $112$ and $120$ usable ones, the shortfall being
the draws on which the boundary kernel drove $\hat\pi$ non-positive at a design
point, so that the adjoint could not be formed and the replication was dropped
rather than returned degraded; the count is a property of the cell and is
identical across the three cardinalities in all nine of them, which is what
leaves the paired contrast defined. At a coverage rate near $0.95$ the Monte
Carlo standard error is about $0.02$, so two of them resolve to about $\pm0.040$
and a gap smaller than that is not evidence of anything. *That is the smallest
resolution in the suite and it is calibrated at one point*: at the misspecified
constant, where coverage runs from $0.277$ to $0.795$, the printed standard
errors are $0.038$ to $0.046$. Every reading below is priced at the standard
error its own cell prints. What the dropped draws could have done is bounded
rather than merely disclosed, and each table carries the bound in its own header
row: at most $0.024$ on the balanced design and at most $0.063$ on the
misspecified one. The selection is real and its direction is known, a draw
surviving when the nonparametric stage behaved, so the printed rates are the
optimistic reading of that interval.

On the balanced design the estimator behaves as the theorem asks at every
cardinality. The bias at $n=1{,}600$ is inside two of its own Monte Carlo
standard errors at all nine cells, the largest being the constant at four cells
at $-0.0200$ $(0.0125)$. The quantity \cref{thm:rootn} makes constant in $n$,
$\sqrt n$ times the simulated standard deviation, falls across the grid at seven
of the nine cells and is larger at $n=1{,}600$ than at $n=400$ at two, both of
them the constant, by $19.19$ and $5.35$ per cent; *neither move is resolved from
flat*, at $1.50$ and $0.45$ of the standard error Panel B prints, which is
computed from the fourth moment rather than from the Gaussian formula because the
realised kurtosis reaches $10.8$ over the suite. Coverage of the nominal $95\%$
interval at $n=1{,}600$ sits between $0.866$ and $0.975$ at all nine cells
(\cref{tab:sim-merged-rootn-balanced}).

*That range is true and it conceals the shape of its own low end.* Three of the
nine cells sit more than two Monte Carlo standard errors below nominal and they
are not scattered: all three are the constant, at $0.882$, $0.866$ and $0.866$
down the three cardinalities. The shortfall does not shrink in $n$ either. At
four cells the constant runs $0.863$, $0.842$ and $0.866$ across the three sample
sizes, which is flat and $2.7$ standard errors under nominal at the largest of
them. What kind of failure that is, the interval answers and the limit law does
not. The mean estimated standard error over the simulated standard deviation is
below one in $77$ of the suite's $81$ cells and below $0.75$ in $18$ of them;
take the coverage a centred normal carrying that ratio would deliver and subtract
the realised coverage, and the difference is inside $\pm0.070$ at all $54$
well-specified cells, at a root mean square of $0.024$ (Table S32 of the
supplement). *The entire well-specified coverage shortfall is the interval's
scale and not the limit law.*

The third design is the one that breaks, and it breaks in the propensity. Its
constant's bias does not fall in $n$ at four cells, running $-0.3040$, $-0.3242$
and $-0.3830$, and $\sqrt n$ times its standard deviation *rises*, $6.031$,
$6.960$ and $8.605$, where the theorem makes it constant; that move is $3.40$ of
its own standard error and so, unlike the two at the balanced design, it *is*
resolved from flat. Coverage of the constant at $n=1{,}600$ is $0.697$ at two
cells, $0.294$ at three and $0.277$ at four, and the paired bias difference
against the binary arm is $-0.2287$ $(0.0226)$ and $-0.2765$ $(0.0241)$, which
are $10.1$ and $11.5$ standard errors and are not a resolution artefact. The two
slope coefficients are untouched, covering between $0.891$ and $0.950$ at every
cardinality at that sample size (\cref{tab:sim-merged-rootn-misspec}). The damage
is therefore confined to the coordinate the propensity enters, and it grows with
the number of cells at the two larger sample sizes. *At $n=400$ it does not*:
coverage there runs $0.795$, $0.661$ and $0.732$ and the bias $-0.1813$,
$-0.3266$ and $-0.3040$, so four cells show less damage than three on both
measures. Both reversals are inside the bound
$\mathrm{SE}\le\mathrm{SE}_3+\mathrm{SE}_4$, at $0.82$ and $0.38$ of it, and
$n=400$ under this design is the thinnest cell in the suite, at $112$ usable
replications.

The stopping rule fails in the same place and in the same direction, and its
constant is where the failure is visible. At the two well-specified designs the
discrepancy rule selects an iterate inside its budget in most replications at
every cardinality, at $1.000$, $0.917$ and $0.875$ on the balanced design at
$n=1{,}600$ and $1.000$, $0.792$ and $0.667$ on the skewed one. At the
misspecified design it selects one in $0.875$ of replications at two cells,
$0.250$ at three and *none at all* at four, and a rule that never fires returns
the cap, which is the configuration Section 6's bootstrap runs under and says so
(\cref{tab:sim-merged-stopping}). *The threshold is not pinned down by the data,
and we do not claim otherwise.* The same table's first block sweeps it on the
abstract design, where moving $\mathsf c_{14}$ by a single factor of three takes
the probability that the rule fires at all from $0.077$ to $0.760$ at $n=500$
under a zero preliminary and from $0.027$ to $0.603$ under a rate-accurate one.
Outside that neighbourhood the rule is degenerate, returning the cap in every
replication of all twelve cells at $\mathsf c_{14}\le10^{-3}$ and one step in
every replication of all twelve at $\mathsf c_{14}\ge10^{-1}$, so it stops in the
interior only inside a window one to seven per cent of the four decades swept,
and that window moves with $n$ (Table S5 of the supplement). What we can say is
that the cap is not an independent cause of the misspecified design's failure.
Run at $\tau_{\mathrm{DP}}=0$, where the rule never fires and the returned
iterate *is* the cap, moving $\bar m$ from $15$ to $100$ at $n=1{,}600$ and
$\mathsf L=4$ raises the misspecified design's integrated squared error from
$0.195$ to $0.488$, at Monte Carlo standard errors of $0.010$ and $0.067$, while
it lowers the balanced design's from $0.091$ to $0.036$. Iterating longer helps
where the propensity is right and hurts where it is wrong.

One hypothesis of \cref{thm:rootn} fails on every design here, and we report it
rather than absorb it. N1 asks that $E[L(\Delta U,\Delta Z)\mid\Delta Z]$ vanish,
which \cref{cor:centarity} types as $p(\mathsf L-1)$ scalar conditions and not
$p$. Measured in population on the weight the engine solves for, the entrywise
defect over $\max_{j,l}\|L_{jl}\|$ runs from $0.531$ to $0.720$ across the nine
design-by-cardinality cells at $n_{\mathrm{solve}}=640$, against a floor of
$7.6\times10^{-14}$ returned by the same code with the conditional dependence
switched off (Table S30 of the supplement). *This is not a defect in
\cref{thm:rootn}.* It sits between the theory and the implementation: the engine
builds $\ell$ in a class over the residual alone and anchors it by subtracting a
constant, and on a location-scale family with a continuum of conditional means
the zero weight is the only member of that class that satisfies N1. The
re-anchoring of Section 4 would restore it at the same $\ell$; the engine does not
build it. Two things this does not establish. It says nothing about Section 6's
data, where the defect is estimated on a panel whose conditional law is unknown,
and it does not show that the theory's own $\ell_\star$ fails N1 here. By
\cref{prp:orthog}(iii) a live defect leaves the moment's $\varrho$-derivative
non-vanishing, so $\hat\varrho$ enters at first order and the sandwich omits a
term that does not shrink; *we report that as consistent with the standard-error
ratio above and not as demonstrated by it*, the correction itself not being
computed here.

Three readings this section does not support. It does not establish that the
shipped engine and the abstract construction agree, because no cell here shares a
sample size with any of the three experiments in the supplement. It does not
establish that the cardinality is harmless at the well-specified designs, because
$112$ to $120$ replications cannot resolve a coverage gap below about $\pm0.04$
and the paired contrasts bound the bias difference rather than the coverage one
(Table S33 of the supplement). And it does not establish that the N1 defect is
what the standard-error ratio measures: the two quantities are set beside each
other rather than fitted to one another.

# Empirical application

Hedonic price regressions read the value of a local amenity off the
cross-section of property values \citep[see][]{rosen1974,bishop2020}, and
regulatory designations are a standard source of exogenous variation in them
\citep[see][]{greenstonegallagher2008}. Air quality is the amenity with the
longest such literature. The regressor of interest is almost always entered
linearly, and we relax that here, on a two-period county panel whose instrument
is discrete because the regulation that generates it is a rule on thresholds.
The section illustrates the estimator of Section 3 and claims nothing beyond the
illustration; what it does not establish is set out in the last subsection
rather than left to be discovered there.

The data are the county panel \citet{chay2005} assembled to measure how the 1970
Clean Air Act Amendments capitalised into property values. The file holds 989
counties. One candidate control, per-capita expenditure on pollution abatement,
is missing in all 989 rows and is dropped as an empty column rather than as item
non-response, which leaves 22 usable controls and not 23; six more are missing
the local-fiscal block, which leaves an analysis sample of $n=983$ (Table S34 of
the supplement).

Write $Y_{ij}$ for the log of county $i$'s median property value in
$j\in\{1970,1980\}$, $X_{ij}$ for its mean concentration of total suspended
particulates in $\mu$g/m$^3$, $W_i$ for its 1975 nonattainment designation, and
$\Delta Z_i$ for an intercept together with $d_Z$ differenced county
characteristics, at $d_Z=5$ throughout. That is the differenced model of
Section 2 term by term: a continuous endogenous scalar entering through
$\vdagger$, a discrete instrument, a differenced control vector, and a county
effect the differencing removes. Descriptive statistics are in Table S35 of the
supplement, where just under a third of the sample is designated, at a mean of
$0.303$. The intercept is not decoration and A4(ii) requires it: read against
A1b(iv), that clause forces $\Delta Z$ to carry exactly one constant coordinate,
which in a differenced equation is the period effect.

The object of economic interest here is $\vdagger$ and not $\theta_\dagger$,
which inverts \cref{thm:rootn}, whose $\sqrt n$ statement is about
$\theta_\dagger$: the structural function is the hedonic price of air quality,
while $\theta_\dagger$ collects coefficients on demographic and fiscal
controls. Which of the two roles carries the question is a property of the
application rather than of the model.

## The instrument

The designation rule fires on either of two triggers: a county is designated if
its annual geometric mean exceeds the standard, or if its second-highest daily
reading does. We read $W$ as the pair of triggers rather than as their
disjunction, which gives a four-valued instrument: $685$ counties trigger
neither, $114$ the bad-day rule alone, $66$ the annual mean alone, and $118$
both, the last three being the cell sizes \cref{tab:app-localise} prints. The
four cells are ordered in baseline particulates and are not ordered in the
decadal change, so they are not a ladder in the regressor; both orderings come
from the same trigger constructor on the same sample and are printed in no
table. The refinement
discards nothing, since the binary reading is the indicator of the first cell's
complement.

The reason for reading the designation at $\mathsf L=4$ is methodological and
not empirical. Four cells are what the rule says, so the binary indicator is a
coarsening of the datum rather than the datum itself, and under A1 the three
contrasts the four cells generate are further restrictions on the same
$\vdagger$, by \cref{prp:localise}. What the extra cells do not buy should be
said in the same breath: not identification, since a coarsening imposes fewer
restrictions; not testability, which is present already at $\mathsf L=2$; and
not instrument strength, since splitting an instrument creates no variation.
What they buy is the decomposition \cref{prp:localise} describes, in which a
piece far from zero at the common fit is a cell where the four-valued reading
conflicts with $\hat\varphi$.

All three cells exceed their own reference, at $p=0.039$ for the bad-day cell,
$0.006$ for the annual-mean cell and $0.003$ for the joint cell, against a null
that redraws $W$ from the fitted propensity (\cref{tab:app-localise}). The
reading runs one way only, since a small $p$ localises a conflict to that cell
while a large one exonerates nothing: consistency across cells is necessary and
not sufficient for A1 by \cref{prp:localise}(iii), and the false-negative rate
of the attribution is unpriced. The table repeats the calculation at the
cross-fitted propensity, and which of the two \cref{prp:localise}'s diagnostic
should use is not settled here. We report the three cells and draw no ordering
from them.

The instrument moves the regressor. Nonattainment lowers the decadal change in
mean particulates by $8.37$ to $9.11\,\mu$g/m$^3$ across the four control sets,
and does so at the $1$ per cent level at every one of them
(\cref{tab:app-firststage}, Panel A). We read that table on the state-clustered
standard error, because designation was made at the level of the Air Quality
Control Region and A0 assumes independent sampling. Clustered, $F$ runs from
$10.6$ with no controls to $13.1$ at the widest set, so the first stage clears
the conventional threshold of ten at every control set, with little room at the
narrowest. Linear instrumental variables
give $-5.519\times10^{-3}$ log points per $\mu$g/m$^3$, which at the 1970 mean
of $66.0\,\mu$g/m$^3$ is an elasticity of $-0.364$, against the $-0.20$ to
$-0.35$ \citet{chay2005} report on this design; it sits just past the more
negative end of that range and reproduces the sign and the order of magnitude
rather than falling inside it.

A4(i) holds in an in-sample fit and binds in the fit the estimator uses. The
multinomial propensity, projected onto the truncation set of \cref{def:hatT} at
$\varepsilon_\varrho=0.01$, has in-sample minimum $\min_l\hat\varrho_l=0.0115$;
over the $29{,}500$ cross-fitted evaluations one estimation run makes, the
projection binds on $0.997$ per cent of them, at a pre-projection minimum of
$4.3\times10^{-5}$, and at the binary coarsening on none
(\cref{tab:app-theta}). Where it binds, A1 holds at $\hat\varrho$ and fails at
the truncated propensity substituted for it, so those evaluations are outside
the assumption; the theory prices that as a bias term rather than excluding it.
The implied covariance clears \eqref{eq:omegafloor} with room, at
$\lambda_{\min}(\hat\Omega)=0.0113$ against $\varepsilon_\varrho/\mathsf
L=0.0025$, so no cells need merging, which matters because merging strengthens
A1b(iii) and gives back the restrictions the refinement was taken for.

The designation in hand is not the designation that was made. Between 1972 and
1978 nonattainment status was assigned at the level of the Air Quality Control
Region, and the county-level variable in this file is an imputation from monitor
readings. \citet{cropper2023} quantify the discrepancy: the estimated reduction
in total suspended particulates attenuates from $10.2$ and $9.1\,\mu$g/m$^{3}$
across their two panels under the official designation to $6.0$ and $7.7$ under
the county-level definition this section adopts. The imputed variable is
admissible here under non-differential misclassification, so that the
probability of a mislabelling does not depend on $\Delta U$ given $\Delta Z$.
Under it $W$ remains valid and is merely less relevant; under the alternative
the estimator is inconsistent rather than imprecise, so no sample size repairs
it. We assume the condition and do not test it.

## The estimator on this panel

One property of the estimator changed between the diagnostics above and the
estimates below, and it is a hypothesis the theory consumes rather than a tuning
choice. The $x$-direction kernel is the supplement's boundary family at $p_K=8$,
which enforces every truncated moment \eqref{eq:truncmom} asks for, and with it
the clause $\int_{\mathcal X}\hat\nu\,dx=0$ that places the adjoint's range
inside $\mathcal V$. The engine it replaces satisfied neither (Table S47 of the
supplement).

\Cref{tab:app-theta} reports $\hat\theta$ at the headline control set, at
$\mathsf L=4$ and at the binary coarsening, on one cross-fitting stream and at a
common truncation level and iteration cap, so the two columns vary the
cardinality alone. The two agree on sign and on order of magnitude at every
coordinate, and we put the agreement no more strongly than that: measured in
units of the four-cell column's own clustered standard error, no coordinate
moves by as much as $0.53$ of a standard error and four of the six move by less
than a quarter of one. That is the expected direction of no effect rather than a null
result: under A1 the surplus contrasts are further restrictions on the same
$\vdagger$, so they buy localisation and not a different answer, and a large
shift would have been evidence against A1 or against the binary estimate. They
do not buy precision either, the clustered standard error being larger in the
four-cell column at per capita income.

Holding the cap fixed across the two columns is what makes them a one-factor
contrast, and that is not a second-order detail: a third arm at the $\bar m=15$
the binary cardinality would itself have set moves that column further than the
cardinality moves it, by $0.1930$ at its largest coordinate, and the two
contrasts are opposite in sign at five of the six coordinates, so a design that
varied both at once would net them against each other (Table S39 of the
supplement).

The standard errors in both columns are conditional on a hypothesis the
estimator does not impose. \Cref{cor:centarity} makes N1 a condition on a
$p\times(\mathsf L-1)$ matrix, hence $p(\mathsf L-1)$ scalar conditions rather
than $p$, and the anchor this estimator removes is a constant per $(j,l)$ rather
than a function of $\Delta Z$, so it imposes no version of N1 beyond the
unconditional one. What the supplement measures is the smallest defect any
constant anchor can reach, and at $\mathsf L=4$ it is not resolvable from zero,
as it is not at either binary arm (Table S41 of the supplement). That is not
evidence of absence but a statement about the power of the check at $n=983$, and
no moment-level diagnostic could have substituted for it, since
$E[\widetilde W_l\hat L_{jl}\mid\Delta Z]=0$ holds automatically under A1
whatever the anchor is. Inference here is conditional on N1, and by
\cref{prp:orthog}(iii) its failure would cost the propensity direction of the
orthogonality, at the full rate $r_n$ and undamped.

\Cref{fig:app-phi} draws $\hat\varphi$ at the headline control set. The curve
drawn is the four-cell fit, and the binary-coarsening curve does not sit on top
of it: at the common cap the sup gap between the two is $0.0327$, or $85$ per
cent of the four-cell curve's own range of $0.0383$, against a root-mean-square
gap of $0.0136$, so the two separate at some points of the support and not on
average. Letting the cap move with the
cardinality instead would put that sup gap at $0.0081$ and license the sentence
that the two cardinalities agree. That number measures nothing: it nets two
effects that nearly cancel, the cap alone moving the binary curve by $0.0380$.

The curve is not monotone, and the sign the hedonic reading asks for is
delivered on part of the support and not on the rest. It rises at $32$ of its
$59$ grid steps and falls at $27$, in four monotone stretches: it descends to
$-0.0174$ at $48.7\,\mu$g/m$^3$, the 28th percentile; climbs to $+0.0150$ at
$68.5$, the 71st; falls to $+0.0001$ at $86.4$, the 89th; and rises again over
the last four steps. Its whole range is $0.0349$, and its largest sustained
movement, at $+1.64\times10^{-3}$ log points per $\mu$g/m$^3$ between the trough
and the peak, runs the wrong way for the hedonic reading.

The linear slope of the preceding subsection delivers $0.380$ log points over
the $68.8\,\mu$g/m$^3$ separating the 5th and the 95th percentiles of $X$, and
the nonparametric estimate's whole range is under a tenth of that. It is nowhere
as steep either: its steepest single descending step is $-3.28\times10^{-3}$, or
$59.5$ per cent of the linear slope. *The two estimates therefore disagree about
the level of the gradient and not only about its shape.* Every sentence of this
reading is a statement about the point estimate: the constant slope is not a
feature of $\hat\varphi$ anywhere on the support, and the sign it imposes fails
on the two rising stretches, which carry $48.8$ per cent of the pooled
distribution of $X$ between them. We do not call that a negative result, because
the envelope of the next subsection is wide enough that nothing here rules a
constant slope out.
