## The bootstrap

Valid uniform inference on $\hat\varphi$ does not exist in this model, and the
obstruction is a property of the estimator rather than of this application.
Uniform bands for ill-posed problems are built on a source condition written in
the spectral calculus of $T^\ast T$ and on completeness of the instrument, and
neither is available here: the operator equation of Section 2 is nonlinear in
$\varphi$, so there is no adjoint in which to write the condition, and a $W$
with four values delivers completeness no more than a two-valued one does
\citep[see][]{severini2006,babiiflorens2025}. Pointwise sets do exist under
nonlinear ill-posedness \citep[see][]{chen2012b}, but they are indexed by a
sieve dimension where the regularisation index of \cref{def:lfstep} is a
Landweber iteration count. We therefore follow the
companion paper \citep{centorrinofeveflorens2019}, which estimates the same
operator equation from a discrete instrument under the same regularisation: a point estimate, a bootstrap band drawn to show variability,
and one sentence saying what the band is not. *The envelope in
\cref{fig:app-phi} illustrates the variability of $\hat\varphi$ and is not a
confidence set. No coverage is claimed for it and none is computed.*

The $99$ replications resample counties with replacement and re-run the
regularisation in each, holding $\hat\theta$ fixed, and the envelope they give
is wide against the curve it surrounds: its median width over the sixty-point
grid is $1.33$ times everything the curve does. Three further schemes ask
whether that width is an artefact of the resampling or a property of the
estimator, since a resample of $n$ counties leaves roughly $37$ per cent of the
draw as duplicates while halving the information: $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ multiplier
weights, which have the same first two moments and the same effective sample
size but duplicate nothing, and subsamples of $621$ and of $492$ distinct
counties. *That comparison is not evaluable, and we report it as such*: the
three criteria that would have separated the two mechanisms are all statements
about the realised stopping index, and that index equals the cap in every
replication of every scheme, because the discrepancy rule of Section 3 is run at
$\tau_{\mathrm{DP}}=0$ here and the patience is set equal to the cap. What the
schemes do show is agreement on the size of the band, the multiplier arm being
$8.1$ per cent narrower over the grid as a whole and wider at the ends of the
support. The five schemes are set out in Table S44 of the supplement, the
multiplier envelope in Table S45 of the supplement, and the eleven levels this
figure draws, together with the bootstrap's convergence record, in Table S43 of
the supplement.

## What the illustration shows

The estimator runs on this panel and returns the two objects it is built to
return: a slope vector with a clustered standard error, at either cardinality of
the instrument, and a structural curve whose shape contradicts the constant
slope the linear specification imposes. That is the whole of what the section
claims.

At $n=983$ it claims nothing about the asymptotics, and there are two reasons
for that rather than one. Evaluated at $(\mu,r)=(2,\tfrac83)$, the
frontier-clearing configuration the Monte Carlo names, the frontier
\eqref{eq:frontier} is met at no control set that also satisfies A4(ii): it
fails once any control is entered, and the one rung at which it holds is the
intercept-only rung, which A4(ii) excludes because at $\alpha=\tfrac12$ the
sieve-entropy condition admits no integer sieve dimension (Table S49 of the
supplement). The second is
the cardinality arm of the Monte Carlo, which finds the limit law's own
remainder failing to vanish at $\mathsf L=4$ on the paper's named design (Table
S22 of the supplement), in a propensity direction whose price this panel cannot
bound because the N1 defect above is not resolvable from zero. The object that
describes this estimator at this sample size is therefore \cref{cor:ratefloor}
and not \cref{thm:rootn}. *The application illustrates the procedure on a design
the method was built for; it does not demonstrate that the asymptotics bind at
this sample size*, and we would rather say so than let the section be read as
though they did.

# Conclusions

In this paper, we estimate the slope vector of a first-differenced partially
linear panel model whose nonparametric argument is a continuous endogenous
regressor and whose only instrument takes finitely many values. Conditional
independence between
the differenced error and the instrument replaces the conditional mean, a Bierens
family converts that restriction into unconditional moments, sieve
Landweber--Fridman regularisation solves the nonlinear equation that results, and
a cross-fitted one-step on a Neyman-orthogonal moment returns a slope vector and
a standard error.

Five results carry the paper.

Identification of $\theta_\dagger$ runs through the mean restriction alone and
needs no source condition and no rank condition beyond nonsingularity of
$E[\Delta Z\Delta Z']$. A moment free of the structural function exists exactly
when the two periods' tilted marginals of the endogenous regressor coincide, so
the partialling-out route is closed here as a property of the differenced design
and not of the estimator. Orthogonality in the structural direction holds if and
only if the representer solves the adjoint equation, which is the range condition
of the linear theory read at a Fréchet derivative. Under A1 every set of
instrument cells admits a common structural function, so a conflict between two
cells refutes A1 and attributes the refutation to the cells that carry it, and
that statement carries no identification hypothesis at any subset of cells. And
the cross-fitted one-step
is $\sqrt n$-consistent and asymptotically normal with a consistent sample
sandwich, whenever the first-stage rate is faster than $n^{-1/4}$.

What the extra cells buy is that attribution and nothing else. They do not buy
identification, a finer instrument making the identification hypothesis weaker
rather than stronger; they do not buy testability, which is present already at
$\mathsf L=2$; and they do not buy instrument strength, since splitting an
instrument creates no variation.

Efficiency is not among them.

The sandwich is the variance the infeasible plug-in would carry at a known
$\vdagger$, plus a positive semidefinite term that does not vanish under overlap,
and no semiparametric efficiency bound is computed for this model. What the
debiasing weight buys is the removal of a first-order bias and not a smaller
variance.

We assume two ingredients of the estimator to exist and construct neither. The
representer estimator $\hat\ell$ is priced by A5(iv) at a rate
$\epsilon_n$ with $\delta_n\epsilon_n=o_P(n^{-1/2})$, and no construction
attaining it is supplied. The preliminary $\hat\varphi^{(0)}$ is needed at a
declared deterministic envelope $\hat\varepsilon_0$ of polynomial order, for
which consistency will not do, and it has no supplier either. Three further
conditions are primitive rather than derived: $\mu$ and $\mathsf R_\ast$, global
identification of $\vdagger$ at A1b(iii), and the sieve display of Lemma L-7 on
the sieve branch of the first-order bias.

The frontier is qualitative, and the Monte Carlo prices what that costs.
Crossing it makes the second-order remainder vanish eventually and says nothing
about where. At the configuration the theory names the turn falls at
$n^{\ast}\approx10^{58}$, the simulated standard deviation clears a
two-standard-error bar only at $n=181{,}019$ in DGP A and only at the smaller of
two equally admissible constants, and nominal $90\%$ intervals under-cover at
$29$ of the $32$ cells; that experiment is in the supplement, and Table S1 of
the supplement carries the standard-error units the sentence reads. What describes a panel
anyone will run is the rate floor of Section 4 and not the $\sqrt n$ statement.
That reading is about the configuration and not about \cref{thm:rootn}: at a
design whose frontier margin is $0.1318$ in place of $0.0060$, and whose
propensity score is no smoother, the same estimator meets the pre-committed
coverage criterion from $n=354$ upward (Table S13 of the supplement) and clears
the standard-deviation ratio's two-standard-error bar from $n=8{,}000$ at the
same constant (Table S19 of the supplement).

The stopping constant is the second open item. It is computable and not
identified, and at this configuration the criterion it thresholds falls by $11$
to $43$ per cent over the whole iteration budget, so the stop is settled almost
entirely by a number the theory does not pin. Whether a Lepskii-balanced rule
should replace it turns on the preliminary: given the discrepancy rule its own
oracle constant, Lepskii is ahead in all three cells started from zero and
behind in all three started from a rate-accurate one.

The third is severe ill-posedness, which the theorem does not reach. Under
exponentially decaying singular values the rate attainable from any source
condition is logarithmic, so the frontier fails at every smoothness of the
propensity score.

We run the estimator in Section 6 on the county panel of \citet{chay2005}, where
the object is the hedonic price of air quality and the instrument is a
nonattainment designation read as the pair of triggers that produces it, at
$\mathsf L=4$. At $n=983$ the frontier fails at every control set an applied
literature would accept (Table S49 of the supplement), so the object that
describes the estimator there is the rate floor and not \cref{thm:rootn}. That section illustrates the procedure on a
design the method was built for, and shows neither that the asymptotics bind at
this sample size nor anything about the Clean Air Act. We take no position on A1
from it.

Future work should focus on constructing the two missing ingredients, since a
representer estimator with a rate and a preliminary with a declared envelope
would discharge the only maintained hypotheses that name an object without
building it. Recovering marginal effects from $\hat\varphi$ is a second step, and
the derivative parameterisation is not the route, since it lowers the source
index below what the frontier requires. A semiparametric efficiency bound for a
model whose nuisance solves an ill-posed nonlinear operator equation is a third,
and a statement uniform in $P$ is a fourth. The latter would need a class on
which the $P$-specific constants are bounded, a uniform first-stage rate at a
random compressed operator, and a Lindeberg condition uniform in $P$.

Valid inference on $\hat\varphi$ is a fifth, and Section 6 locates it. Uniform
bands in ill-posed models are built on a source condition written at an adjoint
and on completeness of the instrument, and a nonlinear equation with a discrete
instrument supplies neither
\citep[see][]{babii2016,severini2006,babiiflorens2025}. \citet{chen2012b} do reach
nonlinearly ill-posed conditional moment models, but index their sets by a
deterministic sieve dimension, while the regularisation index of
\cref{def:lfstep} is the random stopping time of a discrepancy rule. The
mathematics stops in the same place, \citet{monardnicklpaternain2021} delivering
Bernstein--von Mises for nonlinear forward maps at smooth linear functionals
only. Both literatures give valid inference for the regular $\sqrt n$ part and
neither goes past it, so \cref{thm:rootn} sits on that boundary rather than short
of it.

# Supplementary material {.appendix}

Proofs of all results are in the online supplement. The supplement also carries
the statements this article refers to by name and does not print, the
interpretation of each numbered condition, and the smoothness budget in one
table. It repeats the statements printed here, in the same order and under the
same numbers, so that a proof and the result it proves can be read together.

Two pointers appear in the statements above and both name a target in the
supplement rather than numbering one. `Lemma S:sandwich` is the environment
whose label is `lem:sandwich`, and `(S:smdiff)` is the display whose label is
`eq:smdiff`. Each is the name the supplement gives the object, so it is findable
there by the heading it carries.
